items.title: The Plant That Counts to Two
items.text:
The leaf of a Venus flytrap looks like a small open
mouth. Each trap has two halves joined by a hinge, and a
row of bristles runs along their edges like teeth. The
famous scientist Charles Darwin called it "one of the
most wonderful plants in the world."

Venus flytraps grow wild in only one small corner of the
world. They live within about 75 miles of Wilmington,
North Carolina, in wet, sunny grasslands dotted with
tall longleaf pines. Fires often sweep through these
grasslands. Without the fires, trees and shrubs would
gradually spread and shade the little plants from the
sunlight they need.

Like other plants, a flytrap makes most of its food from
sunlight. The soggy soil where it grows, however, is
poor in nutrients, the substances a plant needs to grow
and stay healthy. Insects and other small creatures
supply what the soil cannot.

Catching them requires a clever trap. Near the hinge, on
the inside of the trap, grow a few tiny hairs. A single
touch does nothing at all. But if an ant or a spider
trips two of the hairs, one after the other, within a
few seconds, the trap snaps shut in as little as half a
second. This way, a raindrop or a scrap of blowing leaf
does not fool the plant into closing for no reason. Once
the trap is shut, its meal cannot squeeze out between
the bristles. The leaf then releases special juices that
slowly break the animal down, and the trap may stay
closed for three to twenty days while the plant absorbs
its meal. After about three meals, the trap turns black
and dies.

For a plant called a flytrap, it catches surprisingly
few flies. When scientists studied what the traps
actually capture, they found that most of the meals are
creatures that crawl rather than fly. About a third are
ants, and almost as many are spiders. Fewer than one
meal in twenty is a flying insect.
items.source: Facts verified against the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, "Venus flytrap (Dionaea muscipula)" (fws.gov/species/venus-flytrap-dionaea-muscipula), for its range in the longleaf pine savannas of the Carolinas, its prey (33 percent ants, 30 percent spiders, fewer than 5 percent flying insects), the 3 to 20 days before a trap reopens, and Darwin's words; North Carolina State University, College of Natural Resources, "Five Things About Venus Flytraps" (cnr.ncsu.edu/news/2021/01/five-things-about-venus-flytraps), for the 75-mile radius around Wilmington, the need for frequent fire, photosynthesis and soil nutrients, and the two touches within seconds that spare a raindrop or debris; North Carolina State University Extension, Gardener Plant Toolbox, "Dionaea muscipula" (plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/dionaea-muscipula/), for the two hinged lobes with bristly edges and the insects or spiders whose touch on two hairs snaps them shut; and the Botanical Society of America, "Dionaea muscipula — the Venus Flytrap" (botany.org/home/resources/carnivorous-plants-insectivorous-plants/dionaea-muscipula-the-venus-flytrap.html), for the hinged trap, the hairs near the crease, the hair-like teeth at the edge, closing in as little as half a second, and about three catches before a trap turns black and dies. items.title: Racing Phileas Fogg
items.text:
Nellie Bly, who was born in Pennsylvania in 1864, was a
young reporter for a New York newspaper called the
World. One day she sat down beside her editor's desk and
told him her idea. "I want to go around the world!" In a
popular novel by Jules Verne, a character named Phileas
Fogg makes that trip in eighty days. Bly believed that
she could do it faster.

Her editor liked the idea, so they took it to the
newspaper's business manager. "It is impossible for you
to do it," he said. "In the first place you are a woman
and would need a protector." He added that she would
carry so much baggage that it would slow her down. Bly
was angry. If the newspaper sent a man instead, she told
him, she would start the same day for another newspaper
and beat him. "I believe you would," he said slowly.

A year later, her editor asked if she could leave in two
days. "I can start this minute," she answered. She
bought a single hand-bag and fit everything she needed
inside it.

On November 14, 1889, Bly sailed from Hoboken, New
Jersey, on a steamship called the Augusta Victoria.
Jules Verne had asked to meet her, so after reaching
England she traveled day and night to Amiens, France, to
see him. Then trains and ships carried her through Italy
and Egypt and across Asia. At a ticket office in Hong
Kong, she heard surprising news. A magazine had sent
another reporter, Elizabeth Bisland, to beat her.

Back home, newspaper readers eagerly followed Bly's
progress. She crossed the Pacific Ocean to San
Francisco, and a special train rushed her across the
United States while Bisland fell far behind. On January
25, 1890, the train pulled into Jersey City, New Jersey,
where a large crowd was waiting. Cannons boomed, and
timekeepers stopped their watches. Nellie Bly had
circled the globe in 72 days, 6 hours, 11 minutes, and
14 seconds.
items.source: Facts verified against Nellie Bly's own account, Around the World in Seventy-Two Days (1890), in the University of Pennsylvania Digital Library, A Celebration of Women Writers (digital.library.upenn.edu/women/bly/world/world.html), for her proposal to her editor, the business manager's objection and her reply (quoted in lines 4, 9–11 and 15), the editor's question a year later and her answer (line 17), and the one hand-bag; PBS American Experience, "Around the World in 72 Days" (pbs.org/wgbh/americanexperience/films/world) and its features "Nellie's Milestones" and "Nellie's Big Adventure", for her birth in Pennsylvania in 1864, the sailing from Hoboken on the Augusta Victoria on November 14, 1889, the route, the visit to Jules Verne at Amiens, the news of Elizabeth Bisland in Hong Kong, the special train, and the arrival in Jersey City on January 25, 1890, at 72 days, 6 hours, 11 minutes and 14 seconds; and the Library of Congress research guide on Nellie Bly in Chronicling America (guides.loc.gov/chronicling-america-nellie-bly), for the World, the novel that inspired the trip, and the large crowd at the arrival. Original prose authored for Sheila ISEE.

items.title: Art That Moves
items.text:
Most sculptures stand perfectly still. A statue carved
from marble looks the same today as it did a hundred
years ago, no matter who walks past it. The American
artist Alexander Calder, who was born in 1898, wanted to
change that. "Why must art be static?" he once asked.
"The next step in sculpture is motion."

Calder grew up in a family of artists. His mother was a
painter, and his father and grandfather were sculptors.
Yet Calder first trained as a mechanical engineer, and
as a young man living in Europe he began building a tiny
circus out of wire, cloth, cork, and other everyday
materials. Then he performed it for audiences himself.
He moved the little figures by hand, told the story in
English and French, and supplied the music.

In 1930, Calder visited the studio of the Dutch painter
Piet Mondrian. Mondrian's paintings were made of black
lines and rectangles of bright color on a white
background, and on one wall of his studio he had tacked
up rectangles of colored cardboard. Calder suggested
that it might be fun to make the rectangles swing back
and forth. Mondrian looked very serious. "No, it is not
necessary, my painting is already very fast," he
answered.

The visit stayed with Calder. "This one visit gave me a
shock that started things," he later recalled. He
stopped making figures of people and animals and began
building sculptures out of simple shapes. At first he
used motors and hand cranks to make the shapes move. In
1931 his friend Marcel Duchamp, another artist, gave
these sculptures a name. He called them mobiles, a
French word that can mean both "motion" and "motive."
Soon Calder discovered that the air alone could do the
job of a motor.

Calder kept making mobiles, using little more than
shears, pliers, wire, and painted sheet metal. He
balanced each piece so carefully that a passing breath
of air can set the whole sculpture slowly turning.
items.source: Facts verified against the Whitney Museum of American Art, "Alexander Calder" (whitney.org/artists/215), for his birth in 1898, his father and grandfather as sculptors, his engineering degree, Calder's Circus and how he performed it, the 1930 visit to Mondrian, Duchamp's word, the motors and cranks and then air currents, and his words in lines 5–6; the Calder Foundation, Calder's own account of the visit to Mondrian's studio (calder.org/works/oil-painting/untitled-1930-18), quoted in lines 21–25, with the naming of the mobile in 1931 and its meaning, and its chronology (calder.org/archive/1898-1925/all and calder.org/archive/1926-1930/all) for his mother as a painter and the circus materials; SFMOMA, the Doris and Donald Fisher Collection (fisher.access.sfmoma.org/525/), for the shears, pliers, wire and painted sheet metal and the counterbalanced parts turning in passing air; and the Denver Art Museum (denverartmuseum.org/object/1966.185) for Mondrian's black lines and rectangles of color on a white ground. items.title: The Eyebrow on the Screen
items.text:
My grandfather lives on the other side of the world,
where it is already tomorrow morning while I am eating
dinner. For years we talked on the telephone every
Sunday. His voice always sounded small and crackly, and
I had to imagine the expression on his face.

Last spring my mother mailed him a tablet so that we
could see each other when we talked. The first video
call was a disaster. The screen showed his ear, then the
ceiling fan, then a close-up of one bushy gray eyebrow.
He was pressing the tablet against the side of his head
like a telephone and shouting hello over and over,
wondering why nobody answered.

I decided to teach him, one Sunday at a time. I showed
him how to hold the tablet in front of his face, like a
mirror. I explained that the tiny picture in the corner
was what I could see. The red button gave us the most
trouble. Every time he leaned forward to wave goodbye,
his thumb landed on it, and the call ended before he
could finish. Finally he copied my directions into a
notebook in big block letters and kept it open beside
the tablet.

By summer our conversations looked completely different.
My grandfather carried the tablet into his garden to
show me his tomato plants, which were taller than he
was. He taught me to fold a paper boat, and I taught him
a card trick. Once he called in the middle of the week,
just to show me a rainbow over the rooftops on his
street.

Now his breakfast and my dinner happen at the same
table, in a way. On Sunday evenings I prop our tablet
against the fruit bowl, and he props his against the
teapot. He raises his cup of tea, and I raise my glass
of milk. When it is time to say goodbye, he leans in so
close that the whole screen fills up with one bushy gray
eyebrow.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE; no real person, place or event is named.

items.title: Two Green Backpacks
items.text:
That fall, half the fourth grade at Sadie's school
seemed to own the same green backpack, the one with
orange zippers. Every afternoon the backpacks hung in a
crowded row of hooks in the fourth-grade hallway, and
every afternoon Sadie grabbed hers without looking and
hurried off to catch the bus.

On Thursday, when she sat down at the kitchen table to
start her homework, she unzipped her backpack and found
a stranger's things inside. There was a pencil case
shaped like a fish, a spotted banana, and a thick
sketchbook. On the inside cover, someone had printed
WYATT, ROOM 11 in neat capital letters.

Sadie only meant to look for a phone number. Instead she
found a comic. Page after page, a raccoon in a
detective's coat followed a trail of muddy footprints
through a city of tall, crooked buildings. Every picture
was drawn in pencil, with careful shading, and the
raccoon's eyes narrowed a little more with each new
clue. On the last page, the footprints stopped at the
edge of a bridge. Underneath, in tiny letters, were the
words TO BE CONTINUED.

Sadie read the comic three times before dinner. Only
then did she remember her math worksheet, which was
sitting in her own backpack, wherever that was.

The next morning a boy was waiting outside Room 9,
holding her backpack at arm's length, as if it might
bite him. "Your yogurt leaked," he said.

Sadie held out the sketchbook. "What happens to the
raccoon?"

The boy stared at her for a long moment. Then he opened
the sketchbook to the last page. He began to explain the
plot, faster and faster, waving his hands at the bridge,
the footprints, and a stolen trumpet that nobody in the
city had missed yet.

A week later, Sadie's backpack had a strip of red tape
wrapped around its handle. Wyatt's sketchbook had a new
page, and the words on it were written in two kinds of
handwriting.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE; no real person, place or event is named.
